findings.detail: In its native profile this build emits CTIME_UPDATE (0x0017) for chmod/hardlink/rename-overwrite/unlink and MKNOD_CREATE (0x0016) for special files. The Rust reference's format-1 registry ends at PERMISSION_CHANGE (0x0015); it cannot express a ctime-only advance (it derives ctime from mtime on INODE_SETATTR) or a special-file inode, so it refuses such a volume. Moving the type into the optional space (bit 15) does NOT help: the reference's verify --deep index rebuild and its mount both call known_type(), which hard-errors on an optional type too. The supported interchange profile is ORFS_COMPAT=1 / mount --compat.

The format reserves bit 15 for records a reader 'may skip', but the Rust reference's replay does not implement skipping: verify --deep's Plane-B index rebuild (Index::from_log -> apply_record) and mount both call Record::known_type(), which hard-errors on an optional-unknown type. So an in-bracket optional record is refused ('record type 0xNNNN is optional and has no known semantics'), not skipped. The scan machine (log::TxMachine) does count optional records into the TX_COMMIT bracket, so the bracket is not the obstacle — the replay is.

findings.record: writable open on an in-place torn tail
findings.detail: After a torn frame inside the committed segment, a writable open (Go recover/mount, or Rust mount) creates a new segment at the committed root but leaves the stale torn bytes in the committed segment; BOTH readers then fail with 'torn record in non-final segment 0'. Go and Rust behave identically, so this is a shared recovery defect, not a Rust<->Go divergence. A read-only open recovers correctly (the assertions above).

Go-generated and Rust-generated legacy_v0 segments differ (/src/tests/fixtures/legacy_v0/or.log/0000000000000000.seg /rust-fixtures/legacy_v0/or.log/0000000000000000.seg differ: char 62, line 1). Both are valid and mutually readable, but the builders use different volume UUID, segment size, inode timestamps, TX_BEGIN advisory expected_* fields, and record-header inode stamps; the Go codec is nevertheless byte-exact (roundtrip) on the Rust bytes.
